lesson.title: Beyond a Single Line: Systems of Inequalities
lesson.summary: A system of inequalities pairs two or more inequalities together, and its solution is every ordered pair that makes all of them true at once, typically an entire region rather than a single point.
lesson.body:
A system of inequalities groups two or more inequality statements together, the same way a system of equations groups equations, and asks for every ordered pair that satisfies all of them simultaneously. The building block here is a single inequality, which on its own already has infinitely many solutions, since expressions like y greater than x - 3 are true for a whole half of the coordinate plane, not just for points on one line, unlike a single linear equation which only ever describes a one-dimensional line of points. Combining several such inequalities into one system narrows that half-plane down further, but rarely all the way down to a single point.

This is the key difference from a system of equations. Two equations typically narrow the solution set down to a single point, because each equation restricts the possibilities to a one-dimensional line, and the overlap of two lines is usually just one point. Two inequalities, by contrast, each restrict the possibilities to a two-dimensional half-plane, so their overlap is generally still a two-dimensional region containing infinitely many points, rather than a single ordered pair. This shift, from points to regions, is the central new idea in this topic, and it is the reason a system of inequalities needs its own vocabulary rather than simply reusing the graphing method as it stands.

Consider the system y > x - 3 and y < -x + 4. To test whether the point (1, 1) is a solution, check it against both inequalities separately. First inequality: is 1 greater than 1 - 3? Since 1 - 3 = -2, the question becomes whether 1 is greater than -2, which is true. Second inequality: is 1 less than -1 + 4? Since -1 + 4 = 3, the question becomes whether 1 is less than 3, which is also true. Because both statements hold, (1, 1) satisfies the entire system, and it counts as one solution among the infinitely many points that will make up the full solution set.

Now test a point that fails. Check (5, 5) against the same system. First inequality: is 5 greater than 5 - 3 = 2? Yes, that is true. Second inequality: is 5 less than -5 + 4 = -1? No, 5 is not less than -1, so this statement is false. Because the second inequality fails, (5, 5) is not a solution of the system, even though it satisfied the first inequality perfectly on its own. Exactly as with systems of equations, a point must satisfy every statement in the system, not merely one of them, to count as a solution, and failing even a single inequality is enough to disqualify a point entirely.

Testing points one at a time works, but it is slow and only answers the question for whichever points you happen to check. The next sections show how to picture the entire solution set at once, by graphing each inequality's boundary line and shading the correct side, so that the full collection of solutions becomes visible in a single picture rather than a list of individual checks, which is far more efficient once several points need to be evaluated.
